2.tell: 'gived' is a non-word on-sight reject; the non-word targets participle formation, so the participle 'given' is the likely key

3.tell: 'she' is not a relative pronoun (would make a run-on); 'which' rejects a human antecedent; 'who' is the default subject relative

4.tell: 'over' is a preposition, so the object form 'whom' is required; B is the only option with whom (also has objective 'him')

5.tell: 'whos' is a non-word reject; 'who's' = who is, ungrammatical before a noun; possessive 'whose' is the standard key

7.tell: B is a full clause and C a cleft fragment while A/D are bare NPs, so the blank is a subject slot; picked the plain noun over the possessive

8.tell: comma before 'however,' between clauses is a splice, killing B and C; semicolon pair A/D left, number is a coin flip

9.tell: odd number out: is/has been/was are all singular, 'were' is the lone plural

10.tell: near-twin pair 'satisfying' vs 'about satisfying' (one is the other minus a word); took the unpadded form

12.tell: odd number out: were/have been/are are plural, 'is' is the lone singular

13.tell: '; and' (A) is illegal, D is a comma splice if the clause is independent; semicolon alone is the well-formed join

14.tell: odd number out: are/were/have are plural, 'has' is the lone singular

15.tell: pure punctuation slot; colon is the only mark that can introduce an explanation/list, guessed it over comma/semicolon

16.tell: half of a punctuation pair: two options carry an em dash, so a dash was opened earlier and must be closed; number guessed singular

17.tell: existential 'there was' (B) and the possessive subject 'the mural's colors' (C) are on-sight modifier-item rejects; D is the plain matching subject

18.tell: three non-finite forms vs one finite; infinitive of purpose is the usual key over 'for delivering'

19.tell: odd number out: has been/was/is are singular, 'are' is the lone plural

20.tell: 'it' is an ambiguous-pronoun reject and the possessive 'Dr. Reyes's expertise' is the classic dangling-modifier wrong; picked the bare person

21.tell: ', so, ' is illegal punctuation on sight; among the rest the semicolon is the only legal join of two independent clauses

22.tell: one noun phrase against three clause/gerund forms — the odd structural form is usually the parallel-with-a-noun key

23.tell: pure punctuation slot with no internal cue; comma is the base-rate choice

24.tell: near-twin 'would not miss' vs 'would not have missed'; counterfactual result clause takes the perfect
